_readme: THE most important file in the project. When a student answers wrong, the tutor
names the specific wrong mental model behind THAT answer, then asks them to confirm.
* label must be SPECIFIC. 'Struggles with forces' is worthless. 'Treats constant
velocity as implying a net force' is something a teacher recognises instantly.
* problem_type is the join key. A wrong answer is only matched against
misconceptions sharing the same problem_type as the question.
* wrong_answer_pattern is a regex matched against the student's answer. A hit here
diagnoses with NO llm call - fast, free and deterministic, which is what you want
* every practice item must have at least one misconception whose pattern matches
one of its wrong options, or the demo's best moment falls back to a guess.
scripts/seed.py checks this and refuses to seed if it fails.

misconceptions.label: Treats constant velocity as implying a net force
misconceptions.description: Believes motion itself requires an ongoing force, so a moving object must have a non-zero net force. This is the single most studied misconception in physics education - it is essentially Aristotelian physics, and it survives instruction remarkably well.

misconceptions.label: Uses sine where cosine is required when resolving along the horizontal
misconceptions.description: Applies the trigonometric function by habit rather than by checking which side of the triangle is adjacent to the angle.

misconceptions.label: Adds perpendicular force magnitudes arithmetically instead of using Pythagoras
misconceptions.description: Treats vectors as plain numbers, so 3 N east plus 4 N north becomes 7 N rather than 5 N.

misconceptions.label: Assumes the normal force always equals mg, even on an incline
misconceptions.description: Memorised N = mg from horizontal-surface problems and applies it without resolving the weight along and perpendicular to the slope.

misconceptions.label: Believes heavier objects fall faster even without air resistance
misconceptions.description: Notices the larger gravitational force on the heavier body but not its proportionally larger inertia.

misconceptions.label: Believes friction depends on contact area rather than on the normal force
misconceptions.description: Intuition from everyday experience: a bigger footprint feels like it should grip more.

misconceptions.label: Assumes an upward force acts on a ball while it is moving upward
misconceptions.description: Confuses velocity with force, so an object moving up is assumed to have something pushing it up.

misconceptions.label: Places both action and reaction forces on the same body
misconceptions.description: Picks weight and normal force as a third-law pair because they are equal and opposite, missing that both act on the same object.

misconceptions.label: Uses mass and weight interchangeably
misconceptions.description: Applies the change in g to the mass rather than to the weight, so mass appears to shrink on the Moon.

misconceptions.label: Treats static friction as a fixed value rather than as a maximum
misconceptions.description: Computes mu_s N and reports it regardless of the applied force, instead of recognising that static friction matches the push up to that limit.
